newsitem.title: PERU: Loud explosion heard at Lima embassy residence.
newsitem.headline: Loud explosion heard at Lima embassy residence.

text.p: A loud explosion was heard early on Thursday from the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima where 104 hostages have been trapped for nine days, officials said.
"The explosion came from within the residence at the back part. We are trying to investigate it but we cannot get very close," Nestor Ramos, a police officer at the site, said.

It was not clear whether the explosion came from inside the building or the grounds of the residence. There were no immediate reports of injuries and television images showed no obvious damage to the building.

Witnesses said that before the explosion -- heard at around 1:45 A.M. local time (0645 GMT) -- they saw no unusual movement of police guarding the site. The explosion was followed by silence from within the residence, police and eyewitnesses said.
One television station reported seeing two men running away from the residence compound over nearby roofs shortly after the explosion. This could not be confirmed.
The explosion came hours after Marxist rebels released one sick hostage on Christmas Day, but 104 hostages had to make do with turkey lunch and Catholic mass rather than freedom.
His head slumped to one side, Kenji Hirata, 34, a first secretary at the Japanese embassy in Lima, was pushed out of the residence by Red Cross workers in a wheelchair.

A police ambulance sped Hirata away to a nearby hospital, where he was put on an intravenous drip and treated for dehydration. The Red Cross said his condition was stable but relatives in Japan said they were worried about his health.

Hirata's release brought to two the number of hostages set free in the last three days. The other freed captive was Uruguayan Ambassador Tabare Bocalandro, liberated on Tuesday after his government released two Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) guerrillas from jail.
Furious at the apparent concession, the Peruvian government pulled out its top diplomat in Uruguay. Japan's Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto also criticised Uruguay.
"The Uruguay government has explained that there was no link between the two (release of the two rebels and the Lima hostage issue)," Hashimoto told reporters.
"I don't know whether this is true or not, but in any case it has made a solution of the case difficult," Hashimoto said. "We must not surrender to terrorism."
Japan has around 30 nationals inside the besieged residence, including Ambassador Morihisa Aoki, host of the ill-fated cocktail reception that was stormed by the MRTA rebels.
Foreign Ministry officials said Japan's prime minister and foreign minister were both considering cancelling foreign trips in January because of the continuing hostage crisis.
Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori has flatly rejected all the demands made by the guerrillas and has said they must release the captives and hand over their weapons.

The rebels have vowed not to surrender until the government releases more than 400 MRTA members from Peruvian jails. They also want an end to free-market economic policies and more state support for the country's impoverished majority.

Japanese media covering the crisis speculated that a behind-the-scenes deal might be worked out to allow the MRTA captors to fly to asylum in Cuba after releasing the hostages, but there has been no official word on this.

Malaysian Foreign Minister Abdullah Badawi arrived in Lima early on Thursday to try to secure the release of his country's ambassador to Peru, Ahmad Mokhtar. Abdullah made no statement to journalists on his arrival.
The decision to send the foreign minister sparked rumours in Peru that Malaysia would try to cut a behind-the-scenes deal with the guerrillas holding its envoy.

As speculation over possible government concessions in the crisis swirled around Lima, Congress President Victor Joy Way was quick to deny as totally false a news agency report that the government planned legislation to grant guerrillas an amnesty.
Rebel violence continued elsewhere in Peru when the much larger Shining Path guerrilla group murdered six men from the same family in the early hours of Wednesday, police said.
The killings in a northern province of Peru were probably not related to the siege as the two guerrilla groups follow different communist doctrines and do not operate together, officials said.
